fr:mainmatter.html:p:
A map f:A\to B is a contractible map if each of its fibers is a contractible type. Define
\mathsf {isContrMap}(f) :\equiv \Pi _{y:B}\mathsf {isContr}\bigl (\mathsf {fib}_f(y)\bigr ).
This note follows Chapter 10 of Introduction to Homotopy Type Theory. Contractibility packages existence and coherent uniqueness in a form stable under equivalence.

Saying that a type has an element only expresses existence. Saying that it has exactly one element in a set-theoretic sense is also too rigid for homotopy type theory, because equality itself may contain structure. A contractible type instead chooses a center and continuously identifies every point with that center. It is therefore a singleton up to homotopy.

The same idea applies fiberwise. A fiber records an input together with a path showing that it maps to the chosen output. Contractibility of that fiber says not only that a preimage exists, but that the complete preimage data are coherently unique. This is the homotopical replacement for the conjunction of surjectivity and injectivity.

A type A is contractible if it has a center that is identified with every element of A. Define
\mathsf {isContr}(A) :\equiv \Sigma _{c:A}\Pi _{x:A}(c=x).
A term of \mathsf {isContr}(A) consists of a center c:A and a contraction from c to every x:A.
The unit type is contractible, and every contractible type is equivalent to the unit type. Contractibility is stronger than mere inhabitation because it also controls all identity information.

For any a:A, the singleton type \Sigma _{x:A}(a=x) is contractible with center (a,\text {refl}_a). Its contraction is exactly path induction: every pair (x,p:a=x) is identified with (a,\text {refl}_a). This observation is the prototype for the fundamental theorem of identity types.

Let A be a type equipped with a point a:A. We say that A satisfies singleton induction at a if, for every type family B:A\to \mathcal {U}, the evaluation map
\mathsf {ev}_a: \left (\Pi _{x:A}B(x)\right )\to B(a), \qquad \mathsf {ev}_a(s):\equiv s(a),
has a section. In symbols,
\mathsf {isSingletonInd}(A,a) :\equiv \Pi _{B:A\to \mathcal {U}}\mathsf {sec}(\mathsf {ev}_a^B).
Equivalently, for every B there are
\mathsf {indSing}_a:B(a)\to \Pi _{x:A}B(x)
and a homotopy
\mathsf {compSing}_a: \mathsf {ev}_a\circ \mathsf {indSing}_a\sim \mathsf {id}_{B(a)}.
The computation rule is propositional: it identifies \mathsf {indSing}_a(b,a) with b, rather than requiring judgmental equality.

The principle resembles induction for the unit type, but its computation rule is a path rather than a judgmental equality. Contractibility supplies enough paths to transport a value at the center to every other point; conversely, singleton induction applied to the family x\mapsto (a=x) constructs a contraction.

fr:title.text: Contractibility Is Equivalent to Singleton Induction

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Contractibility Is Equivalent to Singleton Induction

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A type A is contractible if and only if it has a point a:A at which it satisfies singleton induction.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Suppose first that A has center a:A and contraction C:\Pi _{x:A}(a=x). Normalize the contraction by defining
C'(x):\equiv C(a)^{-1}\cdot C(x).
The left inverse law gives q:C'(a)=\text {refl}_a. For a family B:A\to \mathcal {U} and b:B(a), define
\mathsf {indSing}_a(b,x) :\equiv \mathsf {transport}_B(C'(x),b):B(x).
At x=a, applying transport to q:C'(a)=\text {refl}_a, followed by the computation rule for transport along reflexivity, gives
\mathsf {indSing}_a(b,a) =\mathsf {transport}_B(\text {refl}_a,b) =b.
This supplies the required section of evaluation.
Conversely, suppose A has a point a and satisfies singleton induction. Apply it to the family B(x):\equiv (a=x) and the element \text {refl}_a:B(a). The resulting section is
\mathsf {indSing}_a(\text {refl}_a):\Pi _{x:A}(a=x),
which is a contraction of A with center a.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Let f:A\to B and y:B. The fiber of f over y is the type of elements of A equipped with an identification of their image with y:
\mathsf {fib}_f(y) :\equiv \Sigma _{x:A}\bigl (f(x)=y\bigr ).
Thus a term of the fiber is a pair (x,p) with x:A and p:f(x)=y.

A map f:A\to B is a contractible map if each of its fibers is a contractible type. Define
\mathsf {isContrMap}(f) :\equiv \Pi _{y:B}\mathsf {isContr}\bigl (\mathsf {fib}_f(y)\bigr ).

The forward implication needs no coherence improvement: the contraction already compares the chosen center of each fiber with every other point of that fiber. The following proof extracts the section and retraction explicitly.

fr:title.text: Any Contractible Map Is an Equivalence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Any Contractible Map Is an Equivalence

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
For every map f:A\to B, there is a function
\mathsf {isContrMap}(f)\to \mathsf {isEquiv}(f).

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Suppose every fiber of f is contractible. For each y:B, write the center and contraction as
(g(y),G(y)): \mathsf {fib}_f(y), \qquad C_y:\Pi _{z:\mathsf {fib}_f(y)}\bigl ((g(y),G(y))=z\bigr ).
The first components define g:B\to A; the second components have type
G(y):f(g(y))=y.
Hence G:f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B, so (g,G) is a section of f.
It remains to construct a retraction. Fix x:A. The fiber over f(x) contains both its chosen center and the canonical point
(g(f(x)),G(f(x))), \qquad (x,\text {refl}_{f(x)}):\mathsf {fib}_f(f(x)).
Applying the contraction to the canonical point gives
q_x :\equiv C_{f(x)}(x,\text {refl}_{f(x)}): (g(f(x)),G(f(x)))=(x,\text {refl}_{f(x)}).
Apply the first projection to this identity:
H(x) :\equiv \mathsf {ap}_{\mathsf {pr}_1}(q_x):g(f(x))=x.
Therefore H:g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A, so (g,H) is a retraction of f. Pairing the section and retraction yields
\bigl ((g,G),(g,H)\bigr ): \mathsf {sec}(f)\times \mathsf {retr}(f) :\equiv \mathsf {isEquiv}(f).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The converse requires more care. An inverse chooses a plausible center (g(y),G(y)) for each fiber, but the two inverse homotopies need not initially satisfy the compatibility required for equality of dependent pairs. Coherent invertibility records precisely this missing triangle identity.

A map f:A\to B is coherently invertible if it comes equipped with a map g:B\to A, homotopies
G:f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B, \qquad H:g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A,
and a coherence homotopy
K:\Pi _{x:A}\bigl (G(f(x))=\mathsf {ap}_f(H(x))\bigr ).
The type of such data is
\mathsf {isCohInv}(f) :\equiv \Sigma _{g:B\to A} \Sigma _{G:f\circ g\sim \mathsf {id}_B} \Sigma _{H:g\circ f\sim \mathsf {id}_A} \Pi _{x:A}\bigl (G(f(x))=\mathsf {ap}_f(H(x))\bigr ).
Thus the right inverse law at f(x) agrees with the image under f of the left inverse law at x. This is the pointwise, unit-normalized form of the usual coherence G\mathbin {\cdot }f\sim f\mathbin {\cdot }H.

fr:title.text: An Inverse Can Be Made Coherent

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An Inverse Can Be Made Coherent

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Every map with an inverse can be equipped with the structure of a coherently invertible map. That is, there is a function
\mathsf {hasInverse}(f)\to \mathsf {isCohInv}(f).

fr:title.text: A Coherently Invertible Map Is Contractible

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Coherently Invertible Map Is Contractible

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Every coherently invertible map is a contractible map. Explicitly, there is a function
\mathsf {isCohInv}(f)\to \mathsf {isContrMap}(f).

fr:title.text: Any Equivalence Is a Contractible Map

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Any Equivalence Is a Contractible Map

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
For every map f:A\to B, there is a function
\mathsf {isEquiv}(f)\to \mathsf {isContrMap}(f).

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter: An equivalence has an inverse by An Equivalence Has an Inverse. That inverse can be made coherent by An Inverse Can Be Made Coherent, and a coherently invertible map is contractible by A Coherently Invertible Map Is Contractible. Composing these three constructions gives the asserted function.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fiberwise contractibility makes uniqueness explicit and behaves well under pullback and composition. It also prepares the later proof that \mathsf {isEquiv}(f) is a proposition: once a fiber is contractible, there is no meaningful choice left in its center or contraction.
